claims.text: The initial FeNiCrMn single crystal is a fully annealed, disordered FCC solid solution.
The initial material is free of precipitates and secondary phases.
Yielding begins through thermally activated dislocation nucleation and glide rather than through a phase transformation.
The active dislocations glide on FCC {111} planes.
The onset mechanism is governed by the Peierls barrier and solid-solution friction.
Weak strain-rate sensitivity results from a high activation volume associated with overcoming lattice friction.
Configurational disorder and atomic-size mismatch create a high lattice-friction stress in FeNiCrMn.
Configurational disorder and atomic-size mismatch create a large activation volume for dislocation motion.
Thermal activation over lattice friction dominates strain-rate-dependent viscous drag.
Dislocations nucleate at surface steps or internal defects.
Stacking-fault energy and solid-solution friction mediate dislocation mobility.
Yield strength varies significantly with crystal orientation according to the Schmid factor of the primary {111}<110> slip system.
A <111> loading direction gives the highest yield strength, while <001> gives the lowest.
The strain-rate sensitivity exponent remains below 0.05 across 77–600 K.
Yield strength decreases as temperature increases.
No FCC-to-BCC transformation occurs during the elastic-to-plastic transition between 77 K and 600 K.
The FCC phase is thermodynamically stable for this composition over the specified loading conditions and temperature range.
Pure Ni and Cu generally have higher strain-rate sensitivity than the FeNiCrMn HEA.
Pure Ni and Cu have lower cryogenic yield strength than the FeNiCrMn HEA.
Adding sufficiently high Al can shift the alloy toward BCC phase stability.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis rejects FCC-to-BCC transformation and predicts no BCC phase. Therefore, observing BCC at yielding would challenge the proposed dislocation-only hypothesis and favor, rather than falsify, the transformation hypothesis. The stated falsification rule reverses this logic. Moreover, detecting some BCC at yield would not by itself establish that transformation is the primary deformation mode without a phase-fraction or temporal-causality criterion.
